docs.text: A modern Python SDK for quantitative portfolio optimization. Build, backtest, and iterate on any portfolio strategy using a fully modular, plug-and-play architecture.

docs.title: What is PyAlloq?
docs.text:
PyAlloq is a research-grade SDK that gives you all the building blocks you need to go from raw market data to a fully backtested, production-ready portfolio strategy — without writing boilerplate.

Every component is independently swappable. Change your covariance estimator. Try a different allocator. Add a new return estimator. Your backtesting engine stays the same.

from pyalloq_data_connector.yahoo_finance import YahooFinanceClient
from pyalloq.classical.optimizers.risk_parity import RiskParityAllocator
from pyalloq_core.pipeline import StrategyPipeline
from pyalloq_backtest.engine import WalkForwardEngine

data = YahooFinanceClient().get_market_data(
    tickers=["AAPL", "MSFT", "GOOGL", "AMZN", "TSLA"],
    start="2020-01-01", end="2024-01-01"
)

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(allocator=RiskParityAllocator(tickers=data.assets))
results  = WalkForwardEngine(pipeline=pipeline).run(data)

print(results["tear_sheet"])

docs.title: Feature Highlights
docs.text:
• 🎯 5 classical allocators: Equal Weight, Markowitz (Min Vol / Max Sharpe / Max Return), Risk Parity, Risk Budgeting, Max Diversification
  • 🌳 3 graph-based ML allocators: HRP, HERC, NCO — no covariance inversion required
  • 📈 6 return estimators: EWMA, Momentum, Factor, James-Stein, Implied, Black-Litterman
  • 📊 5 covariance estimators: Empirical, EWMA, Ledoit-Wolf, RMT Denoising, Semi-Covariance
  • 🎲 5 Monte Carlo scenario generators: Gaussian, PCA Factor, Filtered Historical Simulation (FHS), GARCH-EVT-Student-\(t\) Copula, and GMM Markov Regimes
  • 🔭 Meucci Entropy Pooling: First- and second-moment views (AbsoluteView, RelativeView, VolatilityView, CovarianceView) with path-dependent CVaR, View-Adjusted MDD, and Probability of Ruin
  • 🔁 3 backtest splitters: Rolling Window, Expanding Window, Purged K-Fold (ML-safe)
  • 💸 2 transaction cost models: Flat Bps, Almgren-Chriss market impact
  • 🔬 Zero-lookahead guarantee via MarketData.validate_alignment() and slice_time()

docs.text:
split(
    data: MarketData,
) -> Generator[tuple[MarketData, MarketData], None, None]

Yields (train_data, test_data) for neural network training.

Source code in src/pyalloq-backtest/src/pyalloq_backtest/splitters.py 
def split(
    self, data: MarketData
) -> Generator[tuple[MarketData, MarketData], None, None]:
    """Yields (train_data, test_data) for neural network training."""

    total_length = len(data.prices)
    fold_size = total_length // self.n_splits
    embargo_size = int(total_length * self.embargo_pct)

    indices = np.arange(total_length)
    dates = data.prices.index

    for i in range(self.n_splits):
        test_start = i * fold_size
        test_end = test_start + fold_size if i < self.n_splits - 1 else total_length

        test_indices = indices[test_start:test_end]
        train_indices_left = indices[: max(0, test_start - embargo_size)]
        train_indices_right = indices[min(total_length, test_end + embargo_size) :]

        train_indices = np.concatenate([train_indices_left, train_indices_right])

        if len(train_indices) == 0:
            continue

        train_dates = dates[train_indices]
        test_dates = dates[test_indices]

        train_data = MarketData(
            prices=data.prices.loc[train_dates],
            features={k: v.loc[train_dates] for k, v in data.features.items()}
            if data.features
            else {},
            cross_sectional=data.cross_sectional,
            risk_free_rate=data.risk_free_rate.loc[train_dates]
            if isinstance(data.risk_free_rate, pd.Series)
            else data.risk_free_rate,
        )

        test_data = MarketData(
            prices=data.prices.loc[test_dates],
            features={k: v.loc[test_dates] for k, v in data.features.items()}
            if data.features
            else {},
            cross_sectional=data.cross_sectional,
            risk_free_rate=data.risk_free_rate.loc[test_dates]
            if isinstance(data.risk_free_rate, pd.Series)
            else data.risk_free_rate,
        )

        yield train_data, test_data

def validate_alignment(self) -> None:
    """
    Ensures Time Series Data aligns perfectly to prevent look-ahead bias.
    """
    for feat_name, df_feat in self.features.items():
        if not self.prices.index.equals(df_feat.index):
            raise ValueError(
                f"Data misalignment: Feature: {feat_name} index does not perfectly match 'prices' index."
            )

    for feat_name, df_feat in self.future_features.items():
        if not self.prices.index.equals(df_feat.index):
            raise ValueError(
                f"Data misaligment: Future feature '{feat_name}' is missing historical dates."
            )

    if isinstance(self.risk_free_rate, pd.Series):
        if not self.prices.index.equals(self.risk_free_rate.index):
            raise ValueError(
                "Data misalignment: 'risk_free_rate' series index does not perfectly match 'prices' index."
            )

def slice_time(
    self,
    end_date: pd.Timestamp,
    lookback: int | None = None,
    horizon_steps: int = 0,
) -> "MarketData":
    """
    Returns a new MarketData instance safely sliced for a backtest window.
    """
    sliced_prices = self.prices.loc[:end_date]
    if lookback is not None:
        sliced_prices = sliced_prices.iloc[-lookback:]

    sliced_features: dict[str, pd.DataFrame] = {}
    for name, feat in self.features.items():
        sliced_feat = feat.loc[:end_date]
        if lookback is not None:
            sliced_feat = sliced_feat.iloc[-lookback:]
        sliced_features[name] = sliced_feat

    sliced_futures: dict[str, pd.DataFrame] = {}
    for name, feat in self.future_features.items():
        if end_date in feat.index:
            loc = feat.index.get_loc(end_date)
            if not isinstance(loc, int):
                raise ValueError(
                    f"Duplicate timestamps found in future_features['{name}']"
                    "Time series indices must be strictly unique."
                )
            start_loc = max(0, (loc - lookback + 1)) if lookback else 0
            end_loc = loc + 1 + horizon_steps
            sliced_futures[name] = feat.iloc[start_loc:end_loc]
        else:
            sliced_futures[name] = feat.loc[:end_date]

    sliced_rf = self.risk_free_rate
    if isinstance(self.risk_free_rate, pd.Series):
        sliced_rf = self.risk_free_rate.loc[:end_date]
        if lookback is not None:
            sliced_rf = sliced_rf.iloc[-lookback:]

    return self.__class__(
        prices=sliced_prices,
        features=sliced_features,
        future_features=sliced_futures,
        cross_sectional=self.cross_sectional,
        risk_free_rate=sliced_rf,
    )

def get_cumulative_returns(self) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    Returns total cumulative asset returns of shape (M, N) over the full horizon,
    incorporating t=0 initial_prices when available.
    """
    final_prices = self.prices[:, -1, :]
    if self.initial_prices is not None:
        init_p = np.asarray(self.initial_prices, dtype=final_prices.dtype)
        return (final_prices - init_p) / init_p
    initial_prices = self.prices[:, 0, :]
    return (final_prices - initial_prices) / initial_prices

def get_path(
    self, path_idx: int, feature_pipeline: object | None = None
) -> MarketData:
    """
    Slices the 3D tensor at index `path_idx` and returns a standard 2D MarketData
    object mathematically compatible with the existing StrategyPipeline.
    """
    path_prices = pd.DataFrame(
        self.prices[path_idx], index=self.timestamps, columns=self.asset_names
    )

    path_features: dict[str, pd.DataFrame] = {}
    for feature_name, feature_tensor in self.features.items():
        # Support for both asset-specific features (M, T, N) and exogenous macro features (M, T, K)
        if feature_tensor.ndim == 3 and feature_tensor.shape[0] == self.n_paths:
            if feature_name in self.feature_columns:
                columns: list[str] | None = self.feature_columns[feature_name]
            elif feature_tensor.shape[2] == self.n_assets:
                columns = self.asset_names
            else:
                columns = None
            path_features[feature_name] = pd.DataFrame(
                feature_tensor[path_idx], index=self.timestamps, columns=columns
            )

    market_data = MarketData(prices=path_prices, features=path_features)
    if feature_pipeline is not None and hasattr(feature_pipeline, "run"):
        market_data = getattr(feature_pipeline, "run")(market_data)
    return market_data

def generate_batches(
    self, n_paths: int, horizon: int, batch_size: int = 1000
) -> Iterator[ScenarioMarketData]:
    """
    Yields simulated ScenarioMarketData in memory-bounded batches.
    """
    if batch_size <= 0:
        raise ValueError("batch_size must be a positive integer.")
    remaining = n_paths
    while remaining > 0:
        current_batch = min(batch_size, remaining)
        yield self.generate(n_paths=current_batch, horizon=horizon)
        remaining -= current_batch

    self,
    tickers: list[str],
    start: dt.datetime,
    end: dt.datetime,
) -> MarketData:
    """
    The orchestrator method. Standardizes whatever chaotic data the vendor
    returns into mathematically pure T x N matrices, perfectly aligned in time.
    """
    raw_dict = self.fetch_raw_data(tickers, start, end)

    closes, volumes, opens, highs, lows = {}, {}, {}, {}, {}
    all_dates = pd.DatetimeIndex([])

    for ticker, df in raw_dict.items():
        df.columns = [str(c).lower() for c in df.columns]

        closes[ticker] = df.get("close", df.get("adj close"))
        if "volume" in df.columns:
            volumes[ticker] = df["volume"]
        if "open" in df.columns:
            opens[ticker] = df["open"]
        if "high" in df.columns:
            highs[ticker] = df["high"]
        if "low" in df.columns:
            lows[ticker] = df["low"]

        dt_index = pd.to_datetime(df.index)
        all_dates = all_dates.union(dt_index)

    all_dates = all_dates.sort_values()

    def build_and_align(series_dict: dict, fill_method: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
        if not series_dict:
            return pd.DataFrame()

        df = pd.DataFrame(series_dict)
        df = df.reindex(all_dates)

        if fill_method == "ffill":
            return df.ffill()
        elif fill_method == "zero":
            return df.fillna(0.0)
        return df

    prices_df = build_and_align(closes, fill_method="ffill")

    features = {}
    if volumes:
        features["volume"] = build_and_align(volumes, fill_method="zero")
    if opens:
        features["open"] = build_and_align(opens, fill_method="ffill")
    if highs:
        features["high"] = build_and_align(highs, fill_method="ffill")
    if lows:
        features["low"] = build_and_align(lows, fill_method="ffill")

    valid_indices = prices_df.dropna(how="all").index
    prices_df = prices_df.loc[valid_indices]

    for key in features:
        features[key] = features[key].loc[valid_indices]

    return MarketData(prices=prices_df, features=features)

def fit(self, data: MarketData, log_returns: bool = False) -> None:
    """
    De-Volatizes the historical time series to extract empirical shocks.
    """
    self.data: MarketData = (
        FactorBackcastImputer().fit_transform(data) if self.impute_missing else data
    )
    self.log_returns = log_returns
    self._record_index_metadata(self.data.prices.index)
    self.initial_prices = self.data.prices.iloc[-1].to_numpy(dtype=self.dtype)
    self.std_residuals = pd.DataFrame(
        index=self.data.prices.index, columns=self.data.assets, dtype=np.float64
    )
    self.N = len(self.data.assets)
    returns = self.data.get_returns(log_returns)
    self._fit_exogenous_features(self.data, returns)

    # Suppress arch convergence warnings for cleaner SDK output
    warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=FutureWarning)
    scale = 100.0
    arch_dist = cast(
        Literal["normal", "t", "skewt"],
        "normal" if self.dist == "Normal" else self.dist,
    )
    for asset in self.data.assets:
        scaled_ret = returns[asset].dropna() * scale
        am = arch_model(
            scaled_ret,
            mean="Constant",
            vol="GARCH",
            p=1,
            q=1,
            dist=arch_dist,
            rescale=False,
        )

        res = am.fit(disp="off")
        params = res.params.copy()
        params["mu"] = params["mu"] / scale
        params["omega"] = params["omega"] / (scale**2)
        self.garch_params[asset] = params

        # z_t = (r_t - mu) / sigma_t (scale cancels out in ratio)
        cond_vol = pd.Series(res.conditional_volatility, index=scaled_ret.index)
        resid_s = pd.Series(res.resid, index=scaled_ret.index)
        self.std_residuals[asset] = resid_s / cond_vol
        # Store the final historical volatility state (unscaled) to seed t=0 of the simulation
        self.last_volatility[asset] = float(cond_vol.iloc[-1]) / scale

    # Drop rows with any NaNs to ensure a perfectly synchronous residual matrix
    self.std_residuals.dropna(inplace=True)
    self.is_fitted = True

def generate(self, n_paths: int, horizon: int) -> ScenarioMarketData:
    """
    Generates forward-looking synthetic paths.
    Args:
        n_paths (int): No. of Monte Carlo scenarios (M).
        horizon (int): Forward time steps to simulate (T).

    Returns:
        ScenarioMarketData: A dataclass wrapping the (M, T, N) tensor.
    """

    if not self.is_fitted:
        raise ValueError(
            "FHS needs to be fitted. Call .fit(data: MarketData) first"
        )

    T_hist = len(self.std_residuals)

    mu = np.array(
        [self.garch_params[a]["mu"] for a in self.data.assets], dtype=self.dtype
    )
    omega = np.array(
        [self.garch_params[a]["omega"] for a in self.data.assets], dtype=self.dtype
    )
    alpha = np.array(
        [self.garch_params[a]["alpha[1]"] for a in self.data.assets],
        dtype=self.dtype,
    )
    beta = np.array(
        [self.garch_params[a]["beta[1]"] for a in self.data.assets],
        dtype=self.dtype,
    )

    Z_hist = self.std_residuals.to_numpy(dtype=self.dtype)
    current_vol = np.tile(
        np.array(
            [self.last_volatility[a] for a in self.data.assets], dtype=self.dtype
        ),
        (n_paths, 1),
    )
    synthetic_returns = np.zeros((n_paths, horizon, self.N), dtype=self.dtype)
    random_indices = np.random.randint(0, T_hist, size=(n_paths, horizon))

    for t in range(horizon):
        idx = random_indices[:, t]
        Z_t = Z_hist[idx, :]
        sim_returns = mu + (current_vol * Z_t)
        synthetic_returns[:, t, :] = sim_returns
        current_var = (
            omega + alpha * (current_vol * Z_t) ** 2 + beta * (current_vol**2)
        )
        current_vol = np.sqrt(np.maximum(current_var, 1e-12)).astype(
            self.dtype, copy=False
        )

    if self.log_returns:
        synthetic_prices = self.initial_prices * np.exp(
            np.cumsum(synthetic_returns, axis=1)
        )
    else:
        synthetic_prices = self.initial_prices * np.cumprod(
            1.0 + synthetic_returns, axis=1
        )

    synthetic_prices = synthetic_prices.astype(self.dtype, copy=False)
    sim_features, feat_cols = self._simulate_exogenous_features(synthetic_returns)

    return ScenarioMarketData(
        prices=synthetic_prices,
        returns=synthetic_returns,
        asset_names=list(self.data.assets),
        initial_prices=self.initial_prices.copy(),
        timestamps=self._build_future_timestamps(horizon),
        features=sim_features,
        feature_columns=feat_cols,
    )

def build(
    self, views: list[ViewType]
) -> tuple[
    np.ndarray | None, np.ndarray | None, np.ndarray | None, np.ndarray | None
]:
    """
    Parses views and returns (A_ineq, b_ineq, C_eq, d_eq).
    Returns None for matrices if no corresponding constraints exist.
    """
    A_ineq: list[np.ndarray] = []
    b_ineq: list[float] = []
    C_eq: list[np.ndarray] = []
    d_eq: list[float] = []

    # Track reference means and volatilities for centering second-moment views
    ref_means: dict[str, float] = {
        name: float(np.mean(self._get_asset_vector(name)))
        for name in self.asset_names
    }
    ref_stds: dict[str, float] = {
        name: float(np.std(self._get_asset_vector(name)))
        for name in self.asset_names
    }

    for view in views:
        if isinstance(view, AbsoluteView) and view.operator == "==":
            if view.asset in self.asset_idx:
                ref_means[view.asset] = float(view.target)

    for view in views:
        if isinstance(view, VolatilityView):
            vec = self._get_asset_vector(view.asset)
            prior_std = float(np.std(vec))
            target_vol = (
                float(view.target_volatility)
                if view.target_volatility is not None
                else prior_std * float(view.multiplier)  # type: ignore[arg-type]
            )
            ref_stds[view.asset] = target_vol

    for view in views:
        if isinstance(view, AbsoluteView):
            condition_vector = self._get_asset_vector(view.asset)
            target_val = float(view.target)
        elif isinstance(view, RelativeView):
            vec_out = self._get_asset_vector(view.asset_outperformer)
            vec_under = self._get_asset_vector(view.asset_underperformer)
            condition_vector = vec_out - vec_under
            target_val = float(view.target)
        elif isinstance(view, VolatilityView):
            vec = self._get_asset_vector(view.asset)
            mean_val = ref_means[view.asset]
            prior_std = float(np.std(vec))
            target_vol = (
                float(view.target_volatility)
                if view.target_volatility is not None
                else prior_std * float(view.multiplier)  # type: ignore[arg-type]
            )
            condition_vector = (vec - mean_val) ** 2
            target_val = target_vol**2
        elif isinstance(view, CovarianceView):
            vec1 = self._get_asset_vector(view.asset_1)
            vec2 = self._get_asset_vector(view.asset_2)
            m1 = ref_means[view.asset_1]
            m2 = ref_means[view.asset_2]
            condition_vector = (vec1 - m1) * (vec2 - m2)
            if view.target_covariance is not None:
                target_val = float(view.target_covariance)
            else:
                target_val = (
                    float(view.target_correlation)  # type: ignore[arg-type]
                    * ref_stds[view.asset_1]
                    * ref_stds[view.asset_2]
                )
        else:
            raise TypeError("Unsupported view type.")

        if view.operator == "==":
            C_eq.append(condition_vector)
            d_eq.append(target_val)
        elif view.operator == "<=":
            A_ineq.append(condition_vector)
            b_ineq.append(target_val)
        elif view.operator == ">=":
            A_ineq.append(-condition_vector)
            b_ineq.append(-target_val)

    A_out = np.vstack(A_ineq) if A_ineq else None
    b_out = np.array(b_ineq, dtype=np.float64) if b_ineq else None
    C_out = np.vstack(C_eq) if C_eq else None
    d_out = np.array(d_eq, dtype=np.float64) if d_eq else None

    return A_out, b_out, C_out, d_out

def fit(
    self,
    A_ineq: np.ndarray | None = None,
    b_ineq: np.ndarray | None = None,
    C_eq: np.ndarray | None = None,
    d_eq: np.ndarray | None = None,
) -> EntropyResult:
    """
    Calculates posterior probability distribution over scenarios.

    Args:
        A_ineq: Shape (K_ineq, M) such that A_ineq @ x <= b_ineq
        b_ineq: Shape (K_ineq,)
        C_eq:   Shape (K_eq, M) such that C_eq @ x == d_eq
        d_eq:   Shape (K_eq,)
    """
    # Determine number of constraints
    k_ineq = len(b_ineq) if b_ineq is not None else 0
    k_eq = len(d_eq) if d_eq is not None else 0
    total_views = k_ineq + k_eq

    if total_views == 0:
        return EntropyResult(
            weights=self.p.copy(),
            prior=self.p.copy(),
            kl_divergence=0.0,
            success=True,
            message="No views supplied; returned prior.",
        )

    # Standardize constraints: stack into joint matrix G = [C; A]
    matrices: list[np.ndarray] = []
    bounds_targets: list[np.ndarray] = []

    if k_eq > 0 and C_eq is not None and d_eq is not None:
        matrices.append(C_eq)
        bounds_targets.append(d_eq)
    if k_ineq > 0 and A_ineq is not None and b_ineq is not None:
        matrices.append(A_ineq)
        bounds_targets.append(b_ineq)

    G = np.vstack(matrices)  # Shape: (V, M)
    targets: np.ndarray = np.concatenate(bounds_targets)  # Shape: (V,)

    # Dual bounds: lambda (equality) is unconstrained (-inf, inf),
    # nu (inequality) is constrained to [0, inf)
    bounds = [(None, None)] * k_eq + [(0.0, None)] * k_ineq
    init_dual = np.zeros(total_views)

    # Dual objective and analytical gradient
    def dual_objective(gamma):
        # gamma is [lambda, nu], shape: (V,)
        # exponent shape: (M,)
        exponent = -np.dot(gamma, G)

        # Log-sum-exp trick to prevent numerical overflow
        max_exp = np.max(exponent)
        weights_unnorm = self.p * np.exp(exponent - max_exp)
        partition_fn = np.sum(weights_unnorm)

        # Dual function value
        dual_val = np.log(partition_fn) + max_exp + np.dot(gamma, targets)

        # Analytical gradient w.r.t gamma: targets - (G @ posterior_probabilities)
        prob = weights_unnorm / partition_fn
        grad = targets - np.dot(G, prob)

        return dual_val, grad

    # Optimize dual problem using L-BFGS-B
    opt_res = minimize(
        fun=dual_objective,
        x0=init_dual,
        method="L-BFGS-B",
        jac=True,
        bounds=bounds,
        options={"ftol": 1e-12, "gtol": 1e-10, "maxiter": 500},
    )

    # Recover posterior probabilities x* algebraically
    optimal_gamma = opt_res.x
    exponent = -np.dot(optimal_gamma, G)
    max_exp = np.max(exponent)
    unnorm_x = self.p * np.exp(exponent - max_exp)
    x_post = unnorm_x / np.sum(unnorm_x)

    kl = np.sum(np.where(x_post > 1e-16, x_post * np.log(x_post / self.p), 0.0))

    return EntropyResult(
        weights=x_post,
        prior=self.p,
        kl_divergence=kl,
        success=opt_res.success,
        message=opt_res.message,
    )

Calculates probability-weighted terminal and path-dependent portfolio metrics across the simulation horizon T.

Source code in src/pyalloq-simulation/src/pyalloq_simulation/core/evaluator.py 
def evaluate(
    self,
    scenario_data: ScenarioMarketData,
    asset_weights: np.ndarray,
    entropy_result: EntropyResult,
    ruin_threshold: float | None = None,
) -> EvaluationMetrics:
    """
    Calculates probability-weighted terminal and path-dependent portfolio metrics
    across the simulation horizon T.
    """
    weights = np.asarray(asset_weights, dtype=np.float64)
    probs = np.asarray(entropy_result.weights, dtype=np.float64)  # Shape: (M,)

    cumulative_asset_returns = scenario_data.get_cumulative_returns().astype(
        np.float64
    )  # Shape: (M, N)
    portfolio_returns = np.dot(cumulative_asset_returns, weights)

    expected_return = float(np.dot(portfolio_returns, probs))

    variance = float(np.dot(probs, (portfolio_returns - expected_return) ** 2))
    volatility = float(np.sqrt(max(variance, 0.0)))
    sharpe = (expected_return - self.rf) / volatility if volatility > 0 else 0.0

    sort_idx = np.argsort(portfolio_returns)
    sorted_rets = portfolio_returns[sort_idx]
    sorted_probs = probs[sort_idx]

    cum_probs = np.cumsum(sorted_probs)
    alpha = 0.05
    tail_idx = np.where(cum_probs <= alpha)[0]

    if len(tail_idx) == 0:
        # Fallback if the very first scenario carries > 5% probability mass
        cvar_95 = float(sorted_rets[0])
    else:
        # Normalize the tail probabilities so they sum to 1.0
        tail_probs = sorted_probs[tail_idx] / np.sum(sorted_probs[tail_idx])
        cvar_95 = float(np.dot(sorted_rets[tail_idx], tail_probs))

    # Path-dependent intra-horizon metrics along axis=1 (time steps 0..T)
    M = scenario_data.prices.shape[0]
    if scenario_data.initial_prices is not None:
        init_p = np.asarray(scenario_data.initial_prices, dtype=np.float64)[
            None, None, :
        ]
        rel_prices = scenario_data.prices.astype(np.float64) / init_p
        # Portfolio wealth at each step t=1..T: (M, T)
        step_wealth: np.ndarray = np.tensordot(rel_prices, weights, axes=([2], [0]))
    else:
        step_port_rets = np.tensordot(
            scenario_data.returns.astype(np.float64), weights, axes=([2], [0])
        )
        step_wealth = np.cumprod(1.0 + step_port_rets, axis=1).astype(np.float64)

    # Prepend t=0 initial portfolio equity = 1.0 -> shape (M, T + 1)
    wealth_curve = np.concatenate(
        [np.ones((M, 1), dtype=np.float64), step_wealth], axis=1
    )
    running_peaks = np.maximum.accumulate(wealth_curve, axis=1)
    drawdowns = (wealth_curve - running_peaks) / np.maximum(running_peaks, 1e-12)
    path_mdds = np.min(drawdowns, axis=1)  # Shape: (M,), values <= 0.0

    view_adjusted_mdd = float(np.dot(probs, path_mdds))

    eff_threshold = (
        -abs(ruin_threshold) if ruin_threshold is not None else self.ruin_threshold
    )
    # Ruin occurs if intra-horizon drawdown or equity drop breaches threshold
    min_equity_return = np.min(wealth_curve - 1.0, axis=1)
    ruin_mask = (path_mdds <= eff_threshold) | (min_equity_return <= eff_threshold)
    probability_of_ruin = float(np.dot(probs, ruin_mask.astype(np.float64)))

    return EvaluationMetrics(
        expected_return=expected_return,
        volatility=volatility,
        sharpe_ratio=sharpe,
        cvar_95=cvar_95,
        view_adjusted_mdd=view_adjusted_mdd,
        probability_of_ruin=probability_of_ruin,
    )

docs.title: Building Blocks
docs.text:
PyAlloq is built around six composable building blocks. Each one has a clean, stable interface. You can swap any block independently without touching the others.

This design lets you answer questions like:

"Does Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage improve my Markowitz backtest?" "Does James-Stein return estimation help HRP more than EWMA?" "What happens if I use Almgren-Chriss costs instead of flat fees?"

...all without rewriting your backtesting code.

docs.text:
Package: pyalloq-data-connector

Fetches raw data from any vendor and normalizes it into a MarketData object. Every connector wraps a different API but returns the same output.

from pyalloq_data_connector.yahoo_finance import YahooFinanceClient

data = YahooFinanceClient().get_market_data(
    tickers=["AAPL", "MSFT", "GOOGL"],
    start="2022-01-01",
    end="2024-01-01",
)

Available connectors: Yahoo Finance, Alpha Vantage, Finnhub, EOD Historical Data.

docs.title: Block 2: MarketData
docs.text:
Package: pyalloq-core

MarketData is the universal data container passed between all blocks. It holds:

Field Type Description prices pd.DataFrame Daily closing prices (rows = dates, cols = assets) features dict[str, pd.DataFrame] Time-series features: volume, macro, technicals, etc. cross_sectional pd.DataFrame \| None Market caps, sector mappings, etc. risk_free_rate pd.Series \| float Constant or time-varying risk-free rate risk_aversion pd.Series \| float 0 = most aggressive, 1 = most conservative

Zero-Lookahead Guarantee

MarketData.validate_alignment() raises an error if any feature index doesn't perfectly align with the price index. MarketData.slice_time(end_date, lookback) creates a safe time-window slice for each backtest period, preventing future data from leaking into the estimation window.

docs.title: Block 6: StrategyPipeline

Package: pyalloq-core

StrategyPipeline is the glue that connects your estimators and allocator into a single callable unit. The backtest engine only knows about StrategyPipeline — it doesn't care which estimator or allocator you've chosen.

from pyalloq_core.pipeline import StrategyPipeline

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=MyAllocator(tickers=...),
    returns_estimator=MyReturnEstimator(),   # optional, defaults to EWMA
    cov_estimator=MyCovarianceEstimator(),   # optional, defaults to Empirical
)

weights = pipeline.generate_weights(data)  # → pd.Series

docs.title: Block 7: WalkForwardEngine
docs.text:
Package: pyalloq-backtest

The engine runs your StrategyPipeline across rolling or expanding historical windows, applying transaction costs on each rebalance. It enforces the zero-lookahead guarantee by slicing MarketData before each pipeline call.

from pyalloq_backtest.engine import WalkForwardEngine

engine = WalkForwardEngine(
    pipeline=pipeline,
    rebalance_freq="ME",                  # monthly
    splitter=RollingWindowSplitter(252),  # 1-year lookback
    cost_model=FlatBpsCostModel(10.0),    # 10bps per trade
)

results = engine.run(data)
# → {"returns": pd.Series, "weights": pd.DataFrame, "tear_sheet": pd.DataFrame}

docs.title: Block 8: Monte Carlo Simulation & Entropy Pooling
docs.text:
Package: pyalloq-simulation & pyalloq-core

Generates 3D \((M, T, N)\) synthetic price and feature tensors (ScenarioMarketData), blends non-Gaussian return and volatility views via EntropyPooler, and executes WalkForwardEngine across all \(M\) paths in parallel via ParallelMonteCarloEngine.

from pyalloq_simulation import GARCHEVTCopulaGenerator
from pyalloq_core.engines import ParallelMonteCarloEngine

gen = GARCHEVTCopulaGenerator(nu=5.0)
gen.fit(data)

mc_engine = ParallelMonteCarloEngine(backtest_engine=engine, max_workers=4)
mc_result = mc_engine.run_batches(gen.generate_batches(n_paths=500, horizon=252, batch_size=100))

docs.title: How They Fit Together
docs.text:
Every portfolio optimization workflow in PyAlloq follows the same linear data flow:

Data Connector → MarketData → [Return Estimator + Covariance Estimator] → Allocator
                                         ↕ (via StrategyPipeline)
                              WalkForwardEngine [+ Splitter + Cost Model]
                                         ↓
                                     TearSheet

This separation of concerns means you can:

  • Change the data source without touching your estimators
  • Change estimators without touching your allocator
  • Change the allocator without touching the backtest engine
  • Change cost models or splitters without changing anything else

docs.title: MarketData
docs.text:
MarketData is the single source of truth for all financial data in PyAlloq. Every building block — estimators, allocators, the backtest engine — consumes and produces MarketData.

Understanding how it works is essential to avoiding look-ahead bias in backtesting.

docs.title: Data Fields
docs.text:
from pyalloq_core.data import MarketData
import pandas as pd

data = MarketData(
    prices=prices_df,                    # required: (T × N) closing prices
    features={"volume": volume_df},      # optional: time-series features
    cross_sectional=market_caps_df,      # optional: static cross-sectional data
    risk_free_rate=0.04,                 # constant or pd.Series
    risk_aversion=1.0,                   # 0 = aggressive, 1 = conservative
)
Field Type Required Description prices pd.DataFrame ✅ Closing prices. Rows = dates, Columns = ticker symbols assets list[str] Auto Auto-inferred from prices.columns if not provided features dict[str, pd.DataFrame] ❌ Named time-series feature matrices. Must share the same DatetimeIndex as prices cross_sectional pd.DataFrame \| None ❌ Cross-sectional data (e.g., market caps, sector labels). Not time-indexed risk_free_rate pd.Series \| float ❌ Annual risk-free rate. Defaults to 0.0 risk_aversion pd.Series \| float ❌ Used by MarkowitzAllocator for MAX_RETURN utility. Defaults to 1.0

docs.title: The Features Dictionary
docs.text:
features is a flexible dictionary of named pd.DataFrame matrices. Use it to attach any time-series signal to your market data:

data = MarketData(
    prices=prices_df,
    features={
        "volume":        volume_df,           # daily traded volume
        "momentum_12m":  momentum_df,         # 12-month momentum signals
        "risk_budgets":  risk_budget_df,      # per-asset risk budgets (for RiskBudgetingAllocator)
        "vix":           vix_df,              # macro features
    }
)

Risk Budgets

RiskBudgetingAllocator reads its target budgets from data.features["risk_budgets"]. This is the standard way to pass allocator-specific inputs through the pipeline.

Almgren-Chriss Cost Model

AlmgrenChrissCostModel requires data.features["volume"] to be set for calculating market impact costs.

docs.title: validate_alignment()
docs.text:
Called automatically at construction time. Raises a ValueError if any feature matrix's index does not exactly match prices.index. This prevents silent data misalignment bugs.

# This raises ValueError immediately — catching the bug at construction, not later
data = MarketData(
    prices=daily_prices,
    features={"macro": weekly_macro_df},  # ❌ weekly index ≠ daily index
)
# ValueError: Data misalignment: Feature: macro index does not perfectly match 'prices' index.

docs.title: slice_time(end_date, lookback)
docs.text:
Creates a new MarketData instance safely sliced up to (and including) end_date. The backtest engine calls this for every rebalance window.

# Inside WalkForwardEngine — what happens at each rebalance date:
window_data = data.slice_time(
    end_date=pd.Timestamp("2023-06-30"),
    lookback=252,  # use 1 year of history
)

# window_data.prices ends at 2023-06-30 — no future data leaks through
weights = pipeline.generate_weights(window_data)

slice_time slices all fields consistently: prices, all features, and risk_free_rate (if a Series). The cross_sectional field is passed through unchanged since it is not time-indexed.

docs.title: Working with MarketData Directly
docs.text:
You can generate returns from prices:

returns = data.prices.pct_change().dropna()

Or select a sub-universe:

us_data = MarketData(
    prices=data.prices[["AAPL", "MSFT", "GOOGL"]],
    risk_free_rate=data.risk_free_rate,
)

docs.title: Design Philosophy
docs.text:
MarketData is intentionally a dumb container, not a class with business logic. This design choice means:

  • All components receive the same type of input
  • There is one canonical data format — no per-component data munging
  • Time alignment is validated once at construction, not repeatedly inside each component
  • The backtest engine can slice the data safely without knowing what's inside it

docs.title: ScenarioMarketData (3D Synthetic Tensors)
docs.text:
For Monte Carlo simulation (pyalloq-simulation), ScenarioMarketData wraps 3D \((M, T, N)\) synthetic price, return, and exogenous feature tensors while providing a zero-copy bridge back to 2D MarketData per path:

from pyalloq_core.data import ScenarioMarketData

# Slice path m into a standard 2D MarketData instance compatible with WalkForwardEngine
path_data = scenario_data.get_path(path_idx=0, feature_pipeline=my_feature_pipeline)

# Compute full-horizon cumulative asset returns (M × N) anchored at t=0 initial_prices
cum_returns = scenario_data.get_cumulative_returns()
Field Type Shape Description prices np.ndarray (M, T, N) Simulated asset price paths returns np.ndarray (M, T, N) Simulated single-step asset returns asset_names list[str] (N,) Ordered ticker symbols initial_prices np.ndarray \| None (N,) \(t=0\) anchor prices from the end of historical data timestamps pd.Index (T,) Forward-projected DatetimeIndex (or RangeIndex) features dict[str, np.ndarray] (M, T, K) Jointly synthesized exogenous feature tensors

docs.title: Swapping Components
docs.text:
Because every component in PyAlloq implements a clean interface, you can swap any piece of the stack with a single line of code — without changing anything else.

This page shows side-by-side examples of the most common swaps.

docs.title: Swapping Covariance Estimators
docs.text:
The covariance estimator has the biggest impact on optimizer stability, especially for Markowitz-family allocators. Try each with the same pipeline and compare results.

Empirical (Default)Ledoit-Wolf ShrinkageRMT DenoisingSemi-Covariance 
from pyalloq.classical.estimators.covariance.empirical import EmpiricalCovariance
from pyalloq_core.pipeline import StrategyPipeline
from pyalloq.classical.optimizers.markowitz import MarkowitzAllocator
from pyalloq_core.enums import ObjectiveFunction

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=MarkowitzAllocator(tickers=data.assets, objective=ObjectiveFunction.MIN_VOLATILITY),
    cov_estimator=EmpiricalCovariance(),  # sample covariance — sensitive to outliers
)

from pyalloq.classical.estimators.covariance.ledoit_wolf import LedoitWolfShrinkage

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=MarkowitzAllocator(tickers=data.assets, objective=ObjectiveFunction.MIN_VOLATILITY),
    cov_estimator=LedoitWolfShrinkage(),  # analytically optimal shrinkage intensity
)

from pyalloq.classical.estimators.covariance.random_matrix_theory import RandomMatrixTheoryEstimator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=MarkowitzAllocator(tickers=data.assets, objective=ObjectiveFunction.MIN_VOLATILITY),
    cov_estimator=RandomMatrixTheoryEstimator(denoise=True, detone=False),
)

from pyalloq.classical.estimators.covariance.semi_covariance import SemiCovariance

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=MarkowitzAllocator(tickers=data.assets, objective=ObjectiveFunction.MIN_VOLATILITY),
    cov_estimator=SemiCovariance(),  # penalizes downside volatility only
)

docs.title: Swapping Return Estimators
docs.text:
For allocators that use expected returns (Max Sharpe, Max Return, Black-Litterman), the choice of return estimator directly impacts weights.

from pyalloq.classical.estimators.returns.classical.ewma import EWMAReturnEstimator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=MarkowitzAllocator(tickers=data.assets, objective=ObjectiveFunction.MAX_SHARPE),
    returns_estimator=EWMAReturnEstimator(),  # exponentially weighted mean
)

from pyalloq.classical.estimators.returns.classical.james_stein import JamesSteinReturnEstimator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=MarkowitzAllocator(tickers=data.assets, objective=ObjectiveFunction.MAX_SHARPE),
    returns_estimator=JamesSteinReturnEstimator(),  # shrinks towards grand mean
)

from pyalloq.classical.estimators.returns.classical.momentum import VolatilityScaledMultiHorizonEstimator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=MarkowitzAllocator(tickers=data.assets, objective=ObjectiveFunction.MAX_SHARPE),
    returns_estimator=VolatilityScaledMultiHorizonEstimator(),  # multi-horizon volatility-scaled z-score
)

from pyalloq.classical.estimators.returns.classical.momentum import ResidualMomentumEstimator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=MarkowitzAllocator(tickers=data.assets, objective=ObjectiveFunction.MAX_SHARPE),
    returns_estimator=ResidualMomentumEstimator(),  # beta-neutralized idiosyncratic momentum
)

from pyalloq.dl.estimators.returns.timesfm import TimesFM3MultivariateReturnEstimator
from timesfm3 import TimesFM3Evaluator

tfm_model = TimesFM3Evaluator.load_pretrained(...)  # Loaded TimesFM 3.0 evaluator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=MarkowitzAllocator(tickers=data.assets, objective=ObjectiveFunction.MAX_SHARPE),

from pyalloq.classical.estimators.returns.classical.implied import ImpliedReturnEstimator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(

    returns_estimator=ImpliedReturnEstimator(),  # reverse-optimization from market weights

docs.text:
The allocator is completely decoupled from estimators and the backtest engine. Swap it freely.

from pyalloq.classical.optimizers.risk_parity import RiskParityAllocator

docs.title: Swapping Backtest Splitters
docs.text:
The splitter controls how the engine partitions history for each rebalance window. Swap it in WalkForwardEngine.

Rolling Window (Default)Expanding Window 
from pyalloq_backtest.splitters import RollingWindowSplitter
from pyalloq_backtest.engine import WalkForwardEngine

engine = WalkForwardEngine(
    pipeline=pipeline,
    splitter=RollingWindowSplitter(lookback_window=252),  # fixed 1-year window
)

from pyalloq_backtest.splitters import ExpandingWindowSplitter

engine = WalkForwardEngine(
    pipeline=pipeline,
    splitter=ExpandingWindowSplitter(min_periods=252),  # grows with all available history
)

docs.text:

from pyalloq_backtest.costs import FlatBpsCostModel

engine = WalkForwardEngine(
    pipeline=pipeline,
    cost_model=FlatBpsCostModel(bps=10.0),  # 10 basis points per trade
)

from pyalloq_backtest.costs import AlmgrenChrissCostModel

# Requires data.features["volume"] to be set
engine = WalkForwardEngine(
    pipeline=pipeline,
    cost_model=AlmgrenChrissCostModel(
        portfolio_aum=1_000_000,
        spread_bps=2.0,
        gamma=0.1,
    ),
)

docs.title: Comparing Strategies Side-by-Side
docs.text:
Run multiple pipelines through the same engine and collect results for comparison:

from pyalloq_backtest.engine import WalkForwardEngine

strategies = {
    "Equal Weight":   EqualWeightAllocator(tickers=data.assets),
    "Risk Parity":    RiskParityAllocator(tickers=data.assets),
    "HRP":            HRPAllocator(tickers=data.assets),
    "Min Volatility": MarkowitzAllocator(tickers=data.assets, objective=ObjectiveFunction.MIN_VOLATILITY),
}

results = {}
for name, allocator in strategies.items():
    pipeline = StrategyPipeline(allocator=allocator)
    engine = WalkForwardEngine(pipeline=pipeline, rebalance_freq="ME")
    results[name] = engine.run(data)

# Compare Sharpe ratios
for name, res in results.items():
    sharpe = res["tear_sheet"].loc["sharpe_ratio", "Value"]
    print(f"{name:<20} Sharpe: {sharpe:.2f}")

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: This guide walks you through building and backtesting a complete portfolio strategy end-to-end.

docs.title: Step 1 — Fetch Market Data
docs.text:
Use a data connector to download prices. All connectors return a standardized MarketData object.

from pyalloq_data_connector.yahoo_finance import YahooFinanceClient

client = YahooFinanceClient()
data = client.get_market_data(
    tickers=["AAPL", "MSFT", "GOOGL", "AMZN", "TSLA"],
    start="2020-01-01",
    end="2024-01-01",
)

print(data.assets)   # ['AAPL', 'MSFT', 'GOOGL', 'AMZN', 'TSLA']
print(data.prices.shape)  # (1006, 5)

docs.title: Step 2 — Choose an Allocator
docs.text:
Pick any allocator from pyalloq.classical.optimizers or pyalloq.ml.optimizers. Every allocator implements the same BaseAllocator interface.

from pyalloq.classical.optimizers.risk_parity import RiskParityAllocator

allocator = RiskParityAllocator(tickers=data.assets)

docs.title: Step 3 — Build a Strategy Pipeline
docs.text:
StrategyPipeline wires together your return estimator, covariance estimator, and allocator. Defaults are EWMA returns and empirical covariance.

from pyalloq_core.pipeline import StrategyPipeline

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(allocator=allocator)

To customize the estimators:

from pyalloq.classical.estimators.covariance.ledoit_wolf import LedoitWolfShrinkage
from pyalloq.classical.estimators.returns.classical.james_stein import JamesSteinReturnEstimator

pipeline = StrategyPipeline(
    allocator=allocator,
    returns_estimator=JamesSteinReturnEstimator(),
    cov_estimator=LedoitWolfShrinkage(),
)

docs.title: Step 4 — Run a Walk-Forward Backtest
docs.text:
WalkForwardEngine runs your pipeline on rolling windows of historical data, rebalancing at a specified frequency, and accounts for transaction costs.

from pyalloq_backtest.engine import WalkForwardEngine

engine = WalkForwardEngine(
    pipeline=pipeline,
    rebalance_freq="ME",  # Monthly rebalancing
)

results = engine.run(data)

docs.title: Step 5 — Inspect Results
docs.text:
The engine returns a dictionary with portfolio returns, daily weights, and a performance tear sheet.

print(results["tear_sheet"])

total_return            1.23
annualized_return       0.21
annualized_volatility   0.14
sharpe_ratio            1.45
maximum_drawdown       -0.18
calmar_ratio            1.17

You can also access the raw returns and weight history:

portfolio_returns = results["returns"]     # pd.Series
weight_history    = results["weights"]     # pd.DataFrame

docs.title: Estimator Mathematics
docs.text: This page covers the mathematical foundations of the return and covariance estimators implemented in pyalloq.

docs.title: Exponentially Weighted Mean (EWMA)
docs.text:
Weights observations exponentially so that recent returns matter more:

\[ \hat{\mu}^{EWMA}_i = \frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T} \lambda^{T-t} r_{i,t}}{\sum_{t=1}^{T} \lambda^{T-t}} \]

where the decay factor \(\lambda = 1 - \frac{2}{\text{span}+1}\).

docs.title: James-Stein Shrinkage
docs.text:
Shrinks each asset's historical mean towards the grand mean of all assets. For \(N \geq 3\) assets, the James-Stein estimator strictly dominates the sample mean in terms of MSE:

\[ \hat{\mu}^{JS} = (1 - w^*) \hat{\mu} + w^* \bar{\mu} \mathbf{1} \]

The optimal shrinkage intensity \(w^*\) is:

\[ w^* = \min\left(1,\; \frac{N-2}{(\hat{\mu} - \bar{\mu}\mathbf{1})^\top \hat{\Sigma}^{-1} (\hat{\mu} - \bar{\mu}\mathbf{1})}\right) \]

where \(\bar{\mu} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i \hat{\mu}_i\) is the grand mean.

docs.title: Implied Returns (Reverse Optimization)
docs.text:
Given observed market-capitalization weights \(w^{mkt}\) and the market risk aversion \(\lambda\), the implied equilibrium excess returns are:

\[ \Pi = \lambda \Sigma w^{mkt} \]

This is the equilibrium prior used in Black-Litterman.

docs.title: Black-Litterman
docs.text:
Combines the market equilibrium prior \(\Pi\) with investor views \((P, Q)\) through Bayesian updating.

Views: \(P \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times N}\) is a view-picking matrix, \(Q \in \mathbb{R}^K\) are the expected view returns, and \(\Omega\) is the uncertainty matrix for the views.

Posterior expected returns:

\[ \mu^* = \left[(\tau\Sigma)^{-1} + P^\top \Omega^{-1} P\right]^{-1} \left[(\tau\Sigma)^{-1} \Pi + P^\top \Omega^{-1} Q\right] \]

Posterior covariance:

\[ \Sigma^* = \Sigma + \left[(\tau\Sigma)^{-1} + P^\top \Omega^{-1} P\right]^{-1} \]

where \(\tau\) is a scalar controlling the uncertainty in the prior (typically 0.01–0.05).

docs.title: Ledoit-Wolf Shrinkage
docs.text:
Shrinks the sample covariance \(\hat{\Sigma}\) towards a structured target \(T\) (e.g., diagonal matrix):

\[ \hat{\Sigma}^{LW} = (1 - \alpha^*) \hat{\Sigma} + \alpha^* \hat{\mu}_{cov} I \]

The optimal shrinkage intensity \(\alpha^*\) is derived analytically by minimizing the Frobenius norm of the estimation error:

\[ \alpha^* = \frac{\delta^2}{\gamma^2} \]

where \(\delta^2\) and \(\gamma^2\) are data-dependent scaling constants derived from the Oracle Approximating Shrinkage (OAS) method.

See: Ledoit & Wolf (2004)

docs.title: Random Matrix Theory (Marchenko-Pastur)
docs.text:
For a random matrix \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times N}\) with i.i.d. entries, the eigenvalue distribution of \(\hat{\Sigma} = \frac{1}{T} X^\top X\) converges to the Marchenko-Pastur distribution with upper bound:

\[ \lambda_+ = \sigma^2 \left(1 + \sqrt{\frac{N}{T}}\right)^2 \]

Any empirical eigenvalue \(\lambda_i < \lambda_+\) is attributable to noise, not signal. The denoising step replaces these with the average noise eigenvalue:

\[ \bar{\lambda}_{noise} = \frac{\sum_{i: \lambda_i < \lambda_+} \lambda_i}{|\{i: \lambda_i < \lambda_+\}|} \]

Then the clean covariance is reconstructed: \(\hat{\Sigma}^{RMT} = V \Lambda_{clean} V^\top\)

The optional detoning step removes the largest eigenvalue (corresponding to the market-wide factor) from the correlation matrix before reconstruction, isolating sector-level correlations.

docs.title: Semi-Covariance
docs.text:
Uses only negative return periods to estimate covariance, focusing on downside co-movement:

\[ \hat{\Sigma}^{semi}_{ij} = \frac{1}{T^-} \sum_{t: r_{i,t} < 0} r_{i,t} \cdot r_{j,t} \]

where \(T^-\) is the count of periods where asset \(i\) had a negative return.

docs.title: EWMA Covariance
docs.text:
Uses exponential weighting to capture time-varying covariance:

\[ \hat{\Sigma}_t = (1 - \lambda) r_t r_t^\top + \lambda \hat{\Sigma}_{t-1} \]

where \(\lambda = 1 - \frac{2}{\text{span}+1}\) is the decay factor. This models volatility clustering observed in financial time series (similar to the RiskMetrics model).

docs.title: Graph-Based Allocator Mathematics
docs.text:
This page covers the mathematical foundations of the hierarchical clustering-based allocators: HRP, HERC, and NCO.

These methods avoid inverting the covariance matrix, making them more numerically stable for large universes and ill-conditioned matrices.

docs.title: Hierarchical Risk Parity (HRP)
docs.text: López de Prado (2016). HRP uses hierarchical clustering on the correlation matrix to build a tree of related assets, then allocates weights top-down through the tree using inverse-variance weighting.

docs.title: Step 1: Distance Matrix
docs.text:
Convert the correlation matrix \(\rho\) into a metric distance matrix:

\[ d_{ij} = \sqrt{\frac{1 - \rho_{ij}}{2}} \]

Properties: \(d_{ii} = 0\), \(d_{ij} = d_{ji}\), \(0 \leq d_{ij} \leq 1\).

docs.title: Step 2: Hierarchical Clustering (Dendrogram)
docs.text:
Apply single-linkage agglomerative clustering to the distance matrix to build a binary tree (dendrogram). At each merge step, the distance between two clusters is:

\[ d(C_1, C_2) = \min_{i \in C_1, j \in C_2} d_{ij} \]

docs.title: Step 3: Quasi-Diagonalization
docs.text: Re-order the assets (leaves of the dendrogram) such that similar assets are adjacent. The resulting reordering makes the covariance matrix approximately block-diagonal.

docs.title: Step 4: Recursive Bisection
docs.text:
Traverse the dendrogram top-down. At each level, split the current cluster into two sub-clusters and allocate capital inversely proportional to their sub-portfolio variances:

\[ w_{left} \leftarrow w_{left} \times \alpha, \quad w_{right} \leftarrow w_{right} \times (1 - \alpha) \]

where the allocation split \(\alpha\) is:

\[ \alpha = 1 - \frac{\tilde{\sigma}^2_{left}}{\tilde{\sigma}^2_{left} + \tilde{\sigma}^2_{right}} \]

and \(\tilde{\sigma}^2_C\) is the variance of the inverse-variance portfolio of cluster \(C\):

\[ \tilde{w}_i = \frac{1/\sigma^2_i}{\sum_{j \in C} 1/\sigma^2_j}, \quad \tilde{\sigma}^2_C = \tilde{w}^\top_C \Sigma_C \tilde{w}_C \]

docs.title: Hierarchical Equal Risk Contribution (HERC)
docs.text:
HERC extends HRP by replacing the inverse-variance cluster weights at each bisection step with equal risk contribution weights within each cluster. This enforces risk parity not just at the asset level but at every level of the hierarchy.

At each cluster node, the intra-cluster weights are the ERC solution:

\[ \min_{y_C \geq 0} \; \frac{1}{2} y_C^\top \Sigma_C y_C - \sum_{i \in C} \ln y_{C,i} \]

The inter-cluster allocation still follows the same recursive bisection as HRP, but using the ERC cluster variance instead of the IVP cluster variance.

docs.title: Nested Cluster Optimization (NCO)
docs.text: López de Prado (2019). NCO applies two-level Markowitz optimization:

docs.title: Step 1: Cluster Detection
docs.text: Apply k-means clustering to the correlation matrix (using the first \(k\) principal components as cluster features) to partition assets into \(K\) clusters.

docs.title: Step 2: Intra-Cluster Optimization
docs.text:
Run a within-cluster Markowitz optimization for each cluster \(C_k\) independently:

\[ w^{intra}_{C_k} = \arg\min_{w \geq 0} w^\top \Sigma_{C_k} w \]

This produces one synthetic "cluster portfolio" per cluster.

docs.title: Step 3: Inter-Cluster Optimization
docs.text:
Build a reduced \(K \times K\) covariance matrix from the cluster portfolio returns, and run a second Markowitz optimization across cluster representatives:

\[ w^{inter} = \arg\min_{u \geq 0} u^\top \Sigma^{cluster} u \]

docs.title: Step 4: Combine
docs.text:
The final weight for asset \(i\) in cluster \(C_k\) is:

\[ w_i = w^{intra}_{i \in C_k} \times w^{inter}_{C_k} \]

docs.title: Monte Carlo & Entropy Pooling Mathematics
docs.text: This page covers the mathematical foundations of the scenario generators, missing-history imputation, Meucci's Entropy Pooling (first- and second-moment views), and path-dependent risk metrics implemented in pyalloq-simulation.

docs.title: 1. PCA Factor Back-Casting Imputation
docs.text:
When asset \(j\) has missing historical observations (e.g., a recent IPO missing \(t \in \mathcal{M}_j\) and observed on \(t \in \mathcal{O}_j\)), FactorBackcastImputer avoids truncating the \(N\)-asset matrix:

  1. Identify anchor assets \(\mathcal{A}\) with coverage \(\ge c_{\min}\) and extract \(K\) orthogonal latent factor series \(F \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times K}\) via Principal Component Analysis on anchor returns.
  2. Estimate ridge-stabilized factor loadings for asset \(j\) on its observed window \(\mathcal{O}_j\):
\[ \hat{\beta}_j = \left(X_{\mathcal{O}_j}^\top X_{\mathcal{O}_j} + \lambda I\right)^{-1} X_{\mathcal{O}_j}^\top r_{j, \mathcal{O}_j}, \quad X_t = [1, F_t] \]
  1. Impute missing returns for \(t \in \mathcal{M}_j\) with matched idiosyncratic residual variance \(\hat{\sigma}_{\epsilon, j}^2\):
\[ \hat{r}_{j, t} = X_t \hat{\beta}_j + \epsilon_{j, t}, \quad \epsilon_{j, t} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \hat{\sigma}_{\epsilon, j}^2) \]
  1. Back-cast pre-IPO prices recursively from the first observed price \(P_{j, t_0}\):
\[ P_{j, t} = \frac{P_{j, t+1}}{1 + \hat{r}_{j, t+1}}, \quad t = t_0 - 1, \dots, 0 \]

docs.title: Filtered Historical Simulation (FHSGenerator)
docs.text:
Filtered Historical Simulation (Barone-Adesi et al., 1999) strips volatility clustering using univariate GARCH(1,1) models while preserving empirical cross-asset dependence and fat tails via non-parametric residual bootstrapping:

\[ r_{i, t} = \mu_i + \epsilon_{i, t}, \quad \epsilon_{i, t} = \sigma_{i, t} z_{i, t} \] \[ \sigma_{i, t}^2 = \omega_i + \alpha_i \epsilon_{i, t-1}^2 + \beta_i \sigma_{i, t-1}^2 \]

At each simulated step \(t\), a random historical date index \(\tau \sim \text{Uniform}\{1, \dots, T_{\text{hist}}\}\) is drawn synchronously across all \(N\) assets, preserving cross-sectional co-movement \(Z_{\tau} = (\hat{z}_{1, \tau}, \dots, \hat{z}_{N, \tau})\).

docs.title: GARCH-EVT-Student-\(t\) Copula (GARCHEVTCopulaGenerator)
docs.text:
To model extreme tail risk and positive lower-tail dependence (\(\lambda_L > 0\)), GARCHEVTCopulaGenerator combines AR(1)-GARCH(1,1) filtration with Extreme Value Theory (McNeil & Frey, 2000) and a Student-\(t\) Copula:

  1. AR(1)-GARCH(1,1) Filtration: Extracts standardized residuals \(z_{i, t} = \epsilon_{i, t} / \sigma_{i, t}\).
  2. Semi-Parametric Generalized Pareto (GPD) Marginals: Given lower and upper quantile thresholds \(u_L, u_U\) at probabilities \(q_L, q_U\), exceedances in the tails follow the Generalized Pareto Distribution:
\[ F_i(z) = egin{cases} q_L \left(1 - G_{\xi_{L,i}, eta_{L,i}}(u_L - z) ight) & z < u_L \ \hat{F}_{ ext{emp}}(z) & u_L \le z \le u_U \ q_U + (1 - q_U) G_{\xi_{U,i}, eta_{U,i}}(z - u_U) & z > u_U \end{cases} \]

where the GPD cumulative distribution function is:

\[ G_{\xi, eta}(y) = 1 - \left(1 + rac{\xi y}{ eta} ight)^{-1/\xi} \]
  1. Student-\(t\) Copula Binding: Uniform marginals \(u_{i, t} = F_i(z_{i, t})\) are mapped via the univariate Student-\(t\) quantile \(t_ u^{-1}(u_{i, t})\) to estimate the copula correlation matrix \(R\) with degrees of freedom \( u\). Lower-tail dependence between assets \(i\) and \(j\) is strictly positive:
\[ \lambda_L = 2 \, t_{ u + 1}\!\left(-\sqrt{ rac{( u + 1)(1 - ho_{ij})}{1 + ho_{ij}}} ight) > 0 \]

docs.title: Gaussian Mixture Markov Regimes (GMMRegimeGenerator)
docs.text:
Models discrete latent market states \(s_t \in \{1, \dots, K\}\) via a \(K\)-component Gaussian Mixture Model:

\[ p(r_t) = \sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k \, \mathcal{N}(r_t \mid \mu_k, \Sigma_k) \]

Historical states are decoded via maximum a posteriori assignment \(\hat{s}_t = \arg\max_k \gamma_{t, k}\), yielding the empirical Markov transition matrix \(P \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times K}\) with entries \(P_{ab} = \mathbb{P}(s_{t} = b \mid s_{t-1} = a)\). Forward paths evolve \(s_{m, t} \sim P_{s_{m, t-1}, \cdot}\) and draw \(r_{m, t} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_{s_{m, t}}, \Sigma_{s_{m, t}})\).

docs.title: 3. Meucci's Entropy Pooling (EntropyPooler & ViewBuilder)
docs.text:
Given \(M\) simulated scenarios with prior probability vector \(p \in \Delta^M\) (typically uniform \(p_m = 1/M\)), Entropy Pooling (Meucci, 2008) finds the posterior probability distribution \(x \in \Delta^M\) that satisfies linear equality and inequality views while minimizing Relative Entropy (Kullback-Leibler divergence):

\[ \min_{x \in \mathbb{R}^M} \mathcal{E}(x \,\|\, p) = \sum_{m=1}^{M} x_m \ln\!\left(\frac{x_m}{p_m}\right) \]

subject to:

\[ A x \le b, \quad C x = d, \quad \mathbf{1}^\top x = 1, \quad x \ge 0 \]

docs.title: Unconstrained Dual Formulation
docs.text:
Rather than solving an \(M\)-dimensional primal problem (\(M \sim 10,000\)), EntropyPooler solves the low-dimensional Lagrange dual over the \(V\) view multipliers \(\gamma = (\lambda, u)\) where \( u \ge 0\):

\[ \min_{\lambda, u \ge 0} \; \ln\!\left(\sum_{m=1}^M p_m \exp\!\left(-[G^ op \gamma]_m ight) ight) + \gamma^ op ext{targets}, \quad G = egin{bmatrix} C \ A \end{bmatrix} \]

The posterior scenario weights are recovered analytically via the log-sum-exp stabilized Boltzmann-Gibbs distribution:

\[ x^*_m = rac{p_m \exp\!\left(-[G^ op \gamma^*]_m ight)}{\sum_{k=1}^M p_k \exp\!\left(-[G^ op \gamma^*]_k ight)} \]

docs.title: First- and Second-Moment View Linearization
docs.text:
Because expectation under the scenario measure is a linear inner product \(\mathbb{E}_x[g(R)] = \sum_{m=1}^M x_m g(R_m)\), both first- and second-moment views are linear in the probability vector \(x\):

Absolute Return View (AbsoluteView):

\[ \sum_{m=1}^M x_m R_{m, i} \;\in\; \{\le, =, \ge\}\; \mu_i^{\text{target}} \]

Relative Return View (RelativeView):

\[ \sum_{m=1}^M x_m (R_{m, i} - R_{m, j}) \;\in\; \{\le, =, \ge\}\; \delta_{ij}^{\text{target}} \]

Volatility View (VolatilityView) — centered around the reference mean \(\bar{\mu}_i\):

\[ \sum_{m=1}^M x_m (R_{m, i} - \bar{\mu}_i)^2 \;\in\; \{\le, =, \ge\}\; \left(\sigma_i^{\text{target}}\right)^2 \]

Covariance / Correlation View (CovarianceView):

\[ \sum_{m=1}^M x_m (R_{m, i} - \bar{\mu}_i)(R_{m, j} - \bar{\mu}_j) \;\in\; \{\le, =, \ge\}\; \rho_{ij}^{\text{target}} \bar{\sigma}_i \bar{\sigma}_j \]

docs.title: 4. Path-Dependent Risk Metrics (ScenarioEvaluator)
docs.text:
Let \(W_{m, t}\) denote the simulated portfolio wealth on path \(m \in \{1, \dots, M\}\) at time step \(t \in \{0, \dots, T\}\) with \(W_{m, 0} = 1\):

Path Maximum Drawdown (\(\text{MDD}_m\)):

\[ \text{MDD}_m = \min_{0 \le t \le T} \frac{W_{m, t} - \max_{0 \le \tau \le t} W_{m, \tau}}{\max_{0 \le \tau \le t} W_{m, \tau}} \le 0 \]

View-Adjusted Maximum Drawdown:

\[ \text{MDD}_{\text{view}} = \sum_{m=1}^M x^*_m \, \text{MDD}_m \]

Probability of Ruin (\(\mathbb{P}_{\text{ruin}}\)) — for critical drawdown threshold \(\theta_{\text{ruin}} < 0\) (e.g., \(-0.30\)):

\[ \mathbb{P}_{\text{ruin}}(\theta_{\text{ruin}}) = \sum_{m=1}^M x^*_m \, \mathbb{I}\!\left(\text{MDD}_m \le \theta_{\text{ruin}}\right) \]

docs.title: Portfolio Theory
docs.text: This page documents the mathematical formulations behind each classical allocator implemented in pyalloq.

docs.title: Markowitz Mean-Variance Optimization
docs.text: Markowitz (1952) introduced the canonical portfolio optimization framework: find the weights \(w\) that minimize portfolio variance for a given level of expected return.

docs.title: Minimum Variance
docs.text:
\[ \min_{w} \; w^\top \Sigma w \quad \text{subject to} \quad \mathbf{1}^\top w = 1, \quad w \geq 0 \]

where \(\Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N}\) is the covariance matrix of asset returns.

docs.title: Maximum Sharpe Ratio
docs.text:
Directly maximizing the Sharpe ratio is non-convex. Tobin's mutual fund separation theorem allows the problem to be recast as a convex quadratic program via the substitution trick:

Let \(y = \kappa w\) where \(\kappa = \frac{1}{(\mu - r_f \mathbf{1})^\top w}\). Then:

\[ \max_{w} \; \frac{(\mu - r_f \mathbf{1})^\top w}{\sqrt{w^\top \Sigma w}} \;\equiv\; \min_{y} \; y^\top \Sigma y \quad \text{s.t.} \quad (\mu - r_f \mathbf{1})^\top y = 1, \quad y \geq 0 \]

Recover weights: \(w^* = y^* / \mathbf{1}^\top y^*\)

docs.title: Maximum Utility (Mean-Variance)
docs.text:
Maximize the mean-variance utility function with a risk aversion parameter \(\lambda\):

\[ \max_{w} \; \mu^\top w - \lambda \cdot w^\top \Sigma w \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \mathbf{1}^\top w = 1, \quad w \geq 0 \]

The risk_aversion field in MarketData controls \(\lambda\).

docs.title: Equal Risk Contribution (Risk Parity)
docs.text:
Maillard, Roncalli & Teïletche (2010) propose portfolios where every asset contributes the same amount of marginal risk to the portfolio.

The marginal risk contribution of asset \(i\) is:

\[ \text{MRC}_i = \frac{\partial \sigma_p}{\partial w_i} = \frac{(\Sigma w)_i}{\sigma_p} \]

The total risk contribution of asset \(i\) is:

\[ \text{TRC}_i = w_i \cdot \text{MRC}_i = \frac{w_i (\Sigma w)_i}{\sigma_p} \]

ERC requires \(\text{TRC}_i = \text{TRC}_j\) for all \(i, j\). This is achieved by solving the equivalent convex problem:

\[ \min_{y \geq 0} \; \frac{1}{2} y^\top \Sigma y - \sum_{i=1}^{N} \ln y_i \]

Then normalize: \(w_i = y_i / \sum_j y_j\)

docs.title: Risk Budgeting
docs.text:
Generalizes ERC by assigning target risk budgets \(b_i \geq 0\) (with \(\sum b_i = 1\)) to each asset:

\[ \min_{y \geq 0} \; \frac{1}{2} y^\top \Sigma y - \sum_{i=1}^{N} b_i \ln y_i \]

When \(b_i = 1/N\) for all \(i\), this reduces to Risk Parity. Pass budgets via MarketData.features["risk_budgets"].

docs.title: Maximum Diversification
docs.text:
Choueifaty & Coignard (2008) define the Diversification Ratio:

\[ D(w) = \frac{w^\top \sigma}{\sqrt{w^\top \Sigma w}} = \frac{\sum_i w_i \sigma_i}{\sigma_p} \]

where \(\sigma_i = \sqrt{\Sigma_{ii}}\) is the individual asset volatility and \(\sigma_p = \sqrt{w^\top \Sigma w}\) is the portfolio volatility.

The maximum diversification portfolio maximizes \(D(w)\), which is equivalent (via the same substitution trick as Max Sharpe) to:

\[ \min_{y \geq 0} \; y^\top \Sigma y \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \sigma^\top y = 1 \]

Recover weights: \(w^* = y^* / \mathbf{1}^\top y^*\)

docs.text: Allocator Optimization Problem Requires Returns?
